body:
Choosing an AI development company comes down to five things: have they shipped the *type* of system you need in production, do they measure success in business outcomes rather than model accuracy, are they transparent about cost and timelines, do they take data security seriously, and will they support the system after launch? Get those five right and you will avoid the two most common outcomes of a bad choice — a demo that never becomes a product, and a build you are stuck paying to maintain.

This guide gives you an evaluation framework you can use on your first calls: the signals that separate serious AI teams from agencies that just relabelled themselves as AI companies, the red flags to watch for, the questions that reveal competence fast, and what a fair quote actually looks like.

## Start with the use case, not the technology

Before you talk to any vendor, write one paragraph describing the outcome you want: what process the system touches, who uses it, what a good result looks like in numbers, and what happens when it gets something wrong. Something like: "Our support team spends 40 hours a week answering the same 30 questions; we want a chatbot that resolves at least half without a human, escalates anything involving refunds, and never invents a policy."

This paragraph does two things. First, it lets you compare vendors against the same brief instead of against their marketing. Second, it immediately exposes the shallow ones — if a company cannot talk concretely about your paragraph after one call, they are selling hours, not outcomes. (If you are still at the "what should we even build" stage, read [What Are AI Agents?](/blog/what-are-ai-agents) for a plain-English map of what is actually possible right now.)

## Signal 1: They have shipped your type of system in production

AI breaks down into very different kinds of work: chatbots, AI agents, retrieval systems ([RAG](/blog/what-is-rag)), voice agents, and workflow automation each fail in different ways. A team that builds excellent marketing chatbots may have no idea how to handle the exception paths of an agent that writes to your CRM.

So ask for specifics, not portfolios:

- "Show me a system you built that does *this type of work* and is live today."
- "What went wrong after launch, and how did you fix it?"
- "How long did it take from first call to production, and what slowed it down?"

Notice what a serious answer sounds like: it includes numbers (resolution rates, volumes), mentions something that broke, and is honest about timelines. Be wary of answers that lean entirely on demos, pilot screenshots, or "we have built over 50 AI solutions" without describing any one of them in depth. A portfolio page of logos tells you they sold projects; a walkthrough of one production system tells you they can run one.

## Signal 2: They talk about outcomes before architecture

The best AI companies start with your business problem; the risky ones start with the technology stack. On a first call, pay attention to which questions you get:

**Good questions:** "What does a correct answer look like for your users?" "What happens today when this process fails?" "How will you measure whether this was worth it?" "What are the edge cases?"

**Warning questions:** "Which LLM do you want to use?" "Do you need fine-tuning?" "On-premise or cloud?" — asked before they understand what you are building.

The second set is not inherently bad, but it is premature. Technology choices in AI are tradeoffs that depend entirely on your data, volume, accuracy requirements and budget. Any vendor that prescribes the stack before understanding the problem is optimising for their convenience, not your result.

## Signal 3: Transparent pricing with a written scope

AI project pricing is notoriously vague, which makes this signal easy to test. Ask every candidate:

- What is included in the build, and what is explicitly excluded?
- What will the monthly running costs be (model usage, platform subscriptions, hosting)?
- What does maintenance cost after launch, and what does it cover?
- What happens if the build takes longer than estimated — who absorbs that?

A trustworthy vendor gives you written answers and ranges. A vendor to avoid gives you a single fixed number with no breakdown, or quotes an hourly rate with no estimate of total hours. Fixed-price-with-scope and time-and-materials-with-estimate are both fine; mystery is not.

To calibrate what "fair" looks like, our cost guides break down real ranges: [AI agent development cost](/blog/how-much-does-it-cost-to-build-an-ai-agent) and [AI automation cost](/blog/how-much-does-ai-automation-cost). If a quote is dramatically below those ranges, something is missing — usually testing, monitoring, or the integration work. If it is dramatically above, ask them to justify it line by line.

## Signal 4: They are honest about data security and compliance

AI systems touch your data — customer conversations, documents, internal knowledge. Before you share anything real with a vendor, they should be able to answer:

- Where does your data get processed, and which third-party services touch it?
- Will your data be used to train the AI provider's models? (This is a real concern with some default API settings.)
- Can they work inside your compliance constraints — SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR — where they apply to you?
- What access controls and logging exist on the built system?

A company that waves this away with "we take security very seriously" and nothing more is a risk. You do not need a vendor with every certification under the sun, but you do need one that has thought about the data flow and can describe it. If your project involves regulated data, ask specifically whether they have shipped a compliant build before, and for whom.

## Signal 5: Post-launch support is designed, not improvised

Most AI builds that fail do not fail at launch — they degrade. Models get updated, data drifts, edge cases surface, integrations change. The question is not whether your system will need attention; it is whether that attention has a plan and a price.

Ask:

- What do you monitor in production (accuracy, uptime, error rates, costs)?
- When something breaks or degrades, who fixes it and how fast?
- What does the handoff look like if we part ways — do we own the code, the prompts, the data?
- Is there a maintenance plan, and what is included versus billed separately?

Be especially wary of vendors whose engagement ends at "delivery". An AI system with no monitoring and no owner becomes a liability within months. If a company cannot describe their support offering clearly, assume you will be finding someone else to support it — and price that into your decision.

## Red flags: when to walk away

Some warning signs should end the conversation on the spot:

- **They promise specific outcomes with certainty** — "we will automate 90% of your support" — before understanding your data and processes. Nobody can promise AI accuracy without seeing the problem.
- **They cannot name a production failure.** Every AI system that has lived in production has broken somehow. A vendor with no war stories has no production experience.
- **The team you meet is not the team that builds.** If the senior people on the call disappear after signing and juniors take over, the quality you bought is not the quality you get. Ask who actually does the work.
- **Everything is a custom build.** If every engagement is a six-figure ground-up build and they never suggest simpler options (templates, existing platforms, phased starts), they are selling what pays them, not what fits you.
- **They push a single AI model or platform for every project.** Model choice should depend on the job. A vendor that is locked into one provider optimises for their partnerships, not your cost and quality.
- **No written scope or acceptance criteria.** If "done" is not defined in writing, it will be redefined in their favour later.

## What a fair engagement looks like

The best AI companies usually work in phases, because AI projects genuinely contain unknowns. A typical healthy structure:

1. **Discovery and scoping** (1–2 weeks, often paid, often credited against the build): they map your process, look at your data, define success metrics, and give you a fixed build quote. The paid part matters — free discovery produces free-quality thinking.
2. **Build in milestones with demos** (4–12 weeks depending on scope): you see working software early and regularly, with acceptance criteria agreed in writing per milestone.
3. **Launch with monitoring** (not "handover and disappear"): accuracy baselines, alerting, and a named owner for issues.
4. **Maintenance with a clear plan**: either a retainer or a per-incident arrangement, with the running costs visible to you.

This is also how you de-risk the relationship: a short paid discovery phase lets you evaluate the team on real work before committing to the full build. A vendor that refuses a phased start and insists on the whole contract upfront is asking you to absorb all their risk.

## When you might not need an agency at all

An honest vendor will sometimes tell you not to hire them, and the pattern is worth knowing yourself:

- **If the task is a standard workflow** — routing form submissions, syncing systems, sending follow-ups — no-code tools like n8n, Make or Zapier may do it without any custom development. Our [platform comparison](/blog/n8n-vs-zapier-vs-make-which-automation-platform) helps you decide.
- **If you have no clear success metric**, you are not ready for an agency. Spend a week defining the outcome first — any serious vendor will ask you for it anyway.
- **If the volume is tiny**, the cost of a custom build may never pay back. Automate only what happens often enough to matter.

Knowing these boundaries also tests vendors: bring up the no-code alternative on the call and see whether they engage honestly or dismiss it. The honest reaction is the one you want in a partner.

## The 10 questions to ask on your first call

Keep this list open during every vendor call. The companies that answer crisply are the ones worth shortlisting:

1. Have you shipped a system like this in production? Walk me through one.
2. What broke after launch, and how did you handle it?
3. How do you define "done" for this project — what are the acceptance criteria?
4. What is included and excluded in the quote, and what are the monthly running costs?
5. Who actually builds it — the people on this call?
6. Which models and platforms would you use, and why those for *our* case?
7. Where does our data go, and how is it protected?
8. What do you monitor in production, and what is your support arrangement?
9. What does the handoff look like — do we own the code, prompts and data?
10. Can we start with a paid discovery phase before committing to the full build?

## Frequently asked questions

### How much should an AI development project cost?

It depends on the type and complexity of the system. Simple workflow automations can start in the low thousands; custom AI agents and retrieval systems typically run from the mid five figures up. The honest answer from any vendor should be a range with a breakdown, not a single number. See our guides to [AI agent development cost](/blog/how-much-does-it-cost-to-build-an-ai-agent) and [AI automation cost](/blog/how-much-does-ai-automation-cost) for realistic ranges by project type.

### How long does it take to build an AI system?

A focused build typically takes 4 to 12 weeks from a signed scope to production, depending on complexity. That excludes the discovery phase (1–2 weeks) and assumes your data and integrations are accessible. Timelines stretch when requirements are vague, when data needs cleaning, or when third-party systems need new API access. Be suspicious of any vendor that promises a complex AI build in under three weeks.

### Should I choose a specialised AI company or a general software agency?

For anything where AI is the core of the product — agents, chatbots, retrieval systems, voice AI — choose a team that ships AI systems regularly. General software agencies can be excellent at the surrounding infrastructure, but AI systems fail in AI-specific ways (prompt design, evaluation, hallucination control, model behaviour changes) that generalist teams encounter for the first time on your project. For a standard app with one AI feature bolted on, a generalist with genuine AI experience can be fine — verify the experience, not the claim.

### Is it better to hire in-house or outsource AI development?

Outsourcing makes sense when you need a working system quickly and do not have AI engineers on staff. Building in-house makes sense when AI is a long-term strategic capability you will iterate on for years. A common middle path: an agency builds the first production version while your team learns the system through a proper handoff. If you outsource, make sure you own the code, prompts and data from day one — otherwise switching later becomes expensive.

### What should be in an AI development contract?

At minimum: a written scope with acceptance criteria per milestone, a fixed or capped price with the running costs itemised, data ownership and confidentiality terms, IP ownership of the code and prompts, a defined support and maintenance arrangement, and an exit clause describing what you receive if the engagement ends. "Done" should be a measurable definition, not a date.

### How do I check whether an AI company is legitimate?

Look for evidence of production systems, not just marketing claims. Ask to see a live system and speak to a client reference. Check whether their team publishes technical writing, open-source work or detailed case studies with numbers. Companies that genuinely ship AI systems usually cannot resist explaining how they built them. Vague portfolios and grand claims with no specifics are the pattern to avoid.

### What is the biggest mistake companies make when hiring AI developers?

Choosing on price alone, or choosing the vendor with the most impressive demo. Demos are the easy part — the hard part is the system working reliably at 2am with real data, edge cases and angry users. The vendors worth hiring are the ones who talk about failure modes, monitoring and maintenance unprompted. If a sales process never mentions what happens after launch, that is your answer.
